raw_text:
The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone therapy for prevention of sudden cardiac death in selected patients with ischemic and nonischemic cardiomyopathy, although the magnitude of benefit varies by substrate, competing comorbidity, and contemporary heart-failure treatment [1-3]. Conventional transvenous ICDs are highly effective but expose patients to intravascular and endocardial-lead complications, including lead fracture, venous occlusion, tricuspid-valve interaction, and systemic infection [4,5]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillation capability while avoiding chronic transvenous hardware [6].

The S-ICD consists of a left lateral pulse generator connected to a parasternal subcutaneous electrode. Sensing vectors are entirely extrathoracic, and therapy is limited to high-energy shocks; the device does not provide chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing. Early human experience demonstrated feasibility and successful ventricular-fibrillation conversion [6]. The pivotal IDE study and early international registries subsequently showed high conversion success, acceptable perioperative safety, and low rates of lead-related failure [7,8]. Longer follow-up from pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS and EFFORTLESS registry cohorts confirmed durable shock efficacy, with most complications occurring early and diminishing as implant technique and programming improved [9,10]. Initial multicenter experience also supported the adequacy of the shock vector across diverse body habitus and cardiac substrates [11].

Patient selection is central. Ideal candidates need defibrillation but not pacing: younger patients, those with difficult venous access, prior device infection, dialysis dependence, congenital heart disease, or inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Preimplant electrocardiographic screening is required because large T waves, low R-wave amplitude, bundle-branch block, or dynamic repolarization changes can produce inappropriate sensing; a minority of patients fail screening, especially during exercise or postural change [12]. Discrimination algorithms compare morphology and rate across sensing vectors, and head-to-head testing has shown favorable supraventricular-tachycardia discrimination compared with older transvenous algorithms [13]. Nevertheless, T-wave oversensing has been the signature mechanism of inappropriate shocks, mitigated by exercise screening, dual-zone programming, vector optimization, and filtering algorithms such as SMART Pass [14,15].

Implant technique has evolved from a three-incision approach to two-incision and intermuscular generator placement. Intermuscular implantation improves cosmesis, stabilizes the can, and may reduce erosion, while careful positioning of the coil and generator is essential for defibrillation safety margin [16]. The PRAETORIAN score formalized post-implant assessment of generator and lead position, helping identify configurations at risk for conversion failure [17]. Routine defibrillation testing remains debated, but it has historically been used more often with S-ICD than with transvenous ICDs because efficacy depends heavily on extrathoracic geometry.

The strongest comparative evidence is the PRAETORIAN randomized trial, in which S-ICD therapy was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [18]. As expected, S-ICD recipients had fewer lead-related complications and systemic infections, whereas transvenous ICD recipients benefited from antitachycardia pacing and pacing options. Observational comparative studies generally align with these findings, showing similar mortality and appropriate-shock rates, fewer lead complications, but more shocks for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia in patients who might otherwise have received antitachycardia pacing [19,20]. In a contemporary primary-prevention population with reduced ejection fraction, the UNTOUCHED trial demonstrated low inappropriate-shock rates when modern programming and sensing filters were applied [21].

Special populations illustrate the device’s niche. In dialysis patients, avoiding the bloodstream is attractive because bacteremia, central venous stenosis, and limited vascular access are common [22]. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and Brugada syndrome, where patients are often young and pacing requirements are uncommon, the S-ICD can be effective, although screening failures and dynamic electrocardiographic changes require attention [23,24]. Pediatric and congenital-heart-disease cohorts show feasibility when vascular preservation is important, but small body size, growth, and complex anatomy complicate implantation and follow-up [25,26]. In inherited arrhythmia syndromes, the device is appealing, but careful programming is necessary because sinus tachycardia, T-wave changes, and atrial arrhythmias may provoke oversensing [27].

Limitations remain. The S-ICD cannot treat recurrent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with painless antitachycardia pacing, cannot support bradyarrhythmias, and cannot deliver resynchronization. Generator size, pocket discomfort, and cosmetic concerns may affect acceptance. Conversely, avoidance of transvenous leads directly addresses a major source of long-term ICD morbidity described in broader ICD complication literature [28]. Current guidelines therefore position the S-ICD as an appropriate alternative for patients needing ICD therapy without pacing indications, particularly when venous access or infection risk favors an extravascular system [29,30]. Future directions include smaller generators, longer battery life, refined sensing, integration with leadless pacing for antitachycardia or bradycardia support, and better tools to individualize the trade-off between extravascular safety and pacing capability.
